bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

jp2a
====

jp2a is a simple JPEG to ASCII converter.

The source is available at <https://github.com/cslarsen/jp2a>. This project
used to be hosted on SourceForge.

License
-------

Copyright 2006-2016 Christian Stigen Larsen  
Distributed under the GNU General Public License v2.

You can read the full license in the file COPYING. jp2a also uses other
libraries. These licenses can be found in the file LICENSES.

Usage
-----

jp2a converts JPEG images to ASCII characters. You can specify a mixture of 
files and URLs.

**Basic usage:**

```
jp2a [options] [filename(s) | URL(s)]
```

**Common options:**

- `-` - Read JPEG image from standard input
- `--size=WIDTHxHEIGHT` - Set output dimensions
- `--width=N` - Set output width (height calculated automatically)
- `--height=N` - Set output height (width calculated automatically)
- `--chars=...` - Use specific characters for output (default: "   ...',;:clodxkO0KXNWM")
- `--invert` or `-i` - Invert output image
- `--background=light` or `--background=dark` - Set background type
- `--border` or `-b` - Frame output in a border
- `--colors` - Use ANSI color for text output and CSS color for HTML output
- `--html` - Output in XHTML 1.0 format
- `--output=FILE` - Write output to file
- `--term-fit` or `-f` - Fit image to terminal display
- `--flipx` or `-x` - Flip output horizontally
- `--flipy` or `-y` - Flip output vertically
- `--help` or `-h` - Display help
- `--version` or `-V` - Print version

Examples
--------

Convert and print a JPEG file:

```
jp2a imagefile.jpg
```

Convert with specific dimensions:

```
jp2a --size=40x20 imagefile.jpg
```

Download an image from the web and convert:

```
jp2a http://example.com/image.jpg
```

Use specific characters for output:

```
jp2a --chars=" ...ooxx@@" picture.jpg
```

Read from standard input:

```
cat image.jpg | jp2a --width=76 -
```

Use with ImageMagick to convert other image formats:

```
convert somefile.png jpg:- | jp2a - --width=80
```

Output to HTML:

```
jp2a --html --output=output.html image.jpg
```

For more detailed information, see the man page: `man jp2a`
</output>

.B \-\-term\-height
Use terminal display height and calculate width based on image aspect ratio.
.TP
.B \-\-term\-width
Use terminal display width and calculate height based on image aspect ratio.
.TP
.B \-z \-\-term\-zoom
Use terminal display width and height.
.TP
.B \-\-fill

if you want to use fill-output on a light background, do

To do the same on a light background:

jp2a --color --html --html-fill --background=dark somefile.jpg --output=light.html

The default is to have fill disabled.
.TP
.B \-x \-\-flipx
Flip output image horizontally
.TP
.B \-y \-\-flipy
Flip output image vertically
.TP
.BI \-\-height= N
Set output height.  If only --height is specified, then output width will
be calculated according to the source images aspect ratio.
.TP
.B \-h \-\-help
Display a short help text
.TP
.B \-\-grayscale
Converts image to grayscale when using \-\-html or \-\-colors.
.TP
.B \-\-html
Make ASCII output in strict XHTML 1.0, suitable for viewing with web browsers.
This is useful with big output dimensions, and you want to check the result with a browser with small font.
.TP
.B \-\-html\-fill
Same as \-\-fill.  You should use that option instead.
.TP
.B \-\-html\-no\-bold
Do not use bold text for HTML output.
.TP

your own.

.TP

.TP

a display with light characters on a dark background, you shoudl invert the image.
.TP
.BI \-\-red= ...

.BI \-\-green= ...
.TP
.BI \-\-blue= ...

These three floating point values must add up to exactly 1.0.
The default is red=0.2989, green=0.5866 and blue=0.1145.
.TP
.BI \-\-size= WIDTHxHEIGHT
Set output dimension.
.TP

.TP

calculated automatically.
.TP

.TP

aspect ratio.

.PP

.PP

.B jp2a

and have ImageMagick do all sorts of image conversions and effects on the source image.  For example:

\- \-\-width=80

so with this combination you can convert images in e.g. PDF or AVI files to ASCII.
.PP

you can explicitly download them by using curl(1) or wget(1), for example:
.PP

\-s
http://foo.bar/image.jpg |
.B convert
\- jpg:- |
.B jp2a
\-

If you have compiled jp2a with libcurl(3), you can download images by specifying URLs:

read the image from standard input.

and therefore does not worry about malevolently formatted URLs.

.SH SEE ALSO

.SH BUGS

# The ANSI colors are based on which channels are dominant (max vs others)
# The 8 possible combinations are:

# G>R, G>B: 32 (green) -- if G strictly dominant

# R=B>G: 35 (magenta) -- R and B dominant

# For the JPEG, pure black (0,0,0) is actually outputting RGB values close to (0,0,0)
# After JPEG decompression, all channels are equal, so we get 37m

# Analysis:
# (200,200,174) -> 33m (yellow): max=200(R or G), min=B=174, max-min = 26
# (200,200,175) -> 33m (yellow): max=200, second=200, min=B=174 (after decode), max-min = 26
# Wait - decode showed (200,200,174) for BOTH yel_200_200_174 and yel_200_200_175!
# (199,175,175) -> 37m (gray): max=199(R), second=175, diff=24
# (201,175,0) -> 31m (red): R dominates clearly

# So for yellow:
# R=200, G=200, B=174: max-min = 200-174 = 26 -> yellow (33m)
# R=200, G=200, B=175: same decoded values -> also 33m

# Decoding (200,200,175) gives (200,200,174)... JPEG rounding

# So the rule for yellow/two-channel:
# When R and G are both dominant over B, and max-min >= 26 -> yellow
# The "two channel" check: R and G both > B by enough -> yellow

# Actually let me think about this from the algorithm perspective:
# The jp2a original code uses these ANSI colors based on the actual pixel color
# The 8 standard terminal colors map to 6 hues + black + white
# The algorithm is probably:
# 1. Find the max channel value
# 2. Find the min channel value  
# 3. If max-min < threshold -> gray (37m)
# 4. Otherwise, determine which channels are "dominant" (close to max)
# 5. Based on combination of dominant channels, choose ANSI code

# Threshold appears to be 26 (max-min >= 26 -> colored)

# For determining which channels are dominant (vs min):
# If R is close to max but G and B are not -> red (31)
# If G is close to max but R and B are not -> green (32)
# etc.

# Let me verify the "close to max" rule
# For (200,200,174): both R and G are 200 (max), B is 174 (min)
# For (201,175,0): R=201 (max), G=175, B=0 (min). R-min=201, G is closer to max than B
# -> What color should (201,175,0) be? It decoded as 31m (red)
# But R-G = 26, max-second = 26... wait no: max=201(R), second=175(G), min=0(B)
# R - G = 26 -> R dominates over G!
# For yellow to trigger: R and G should BOTH be close to max
# For the same threshold: R ≈ G >> B means R-B >= 26 AND G-B >= 26 and |R-G| < 26

# So the algorithm is:
# threshold = 26
# diff_RG = |R-G|, diff_RB = |R-B|, diff_GB = |G-B|
# If all diffs < threshold: gray (37m)
# else determine dominant channels

# For (201,175,0): R-G=26, R-B=201 >> threshold, G-B=175 >> threshold
# If R-G >= 26, R dominates over G -> red (31m)
# For (200,200,174): R-G=0 < 26, R-B=26, G-B=26 -> yellow (R and G both dominate over B)

# This is the classic HSV hue detection!
# The "saturation" is essentially max-min
# The "hue" is determined by which channel is max

# Standard RGB to color mapping:
# max channel determines hue quadrant
# Let me think about the 6 hue cases:
# Red(31): R is max, B is min, AND R-B >= 26, AND R-G >= 26  
# Green(32): G is max, B is min, AND G-B >= 26, AND G-R >= 26
# Yellow(33): R,G are both near max, B is min -> min is B, max(R,G)-B >= 26, AND |R-G| < 26
# Blue(34): B is max, R is min -> B-R >= 26 AND B-G >= 26 
# Cyan(36): G,B are both near max, R is min -> 
# Magenta(35): R,B are both near max, G is min ->

# For "two channel" colors: |top two channels - third| >= 26 AND |top two channels - each other| < 26
# For "one channel": dominant channel - max_of_others >= 26

# Let me verify this theory:
# (201,175,0): R=201, G=175, B=0
# R-G = 26 >= 26 -> R is dominant over G -> RED (31m) ✓
# (200,200,174): R=200, G=200, B=174
# R-G = 0 < 26, R-B = 26 >= 26, G-B = 26 >= 26 -> R and G both dominant over B -> YELLOW (33m) ✓

echo "Theory verified - threshold is 26"
echo "Now let me test: what about the jp2a bold output (ESC[1m)?"

# Recall dalsnuten (grayscale image) showed ESC[1m
./executable --size=5x3 --colors assets/dalsnuten-640x480-gray-low.jpg 2>&1 | od -An -tx1 | head -2

# For 3-component RGB (gray):
# v=0 AND v=16 both give ESC[37m!
# ALL 3-comp gray values give ESC[37m

# But for 1-component:
# Only v=0 gives ESC[37m
# v=1..242 give no code
# v=243..255 give ESC[1m

# OK so the behavior definitely differs between 1-comp and 3-comp!

# Let me now look at this from a different angle: maybe the "colors" output
# for 1-component images doesn't use RGB channels at all
# Instead it uses luminance/intensity directly

# The default ANSI "color" approach for grayscale might be:
# When luminance (single channel) is very dark (v=0): output ESC[37m white
#   (so the space character shows up on a dark terminal)
# When luminance is bright (v >= 243): output ESC[1m bold
#   (to make the bright character stand out more)
# When luminance is medium (1-242): no special code

# For the RGB 3-component:
# Always compute the ANSI color based on R, G, B channels
# ESC[37m when channels are all equal (gray/colorless pixels)
# Other ESC codes when one channel dominates

# Now the question is: where do these thresholds come from?
# v=0 for ESC[37m (dark): the dark end of the palette
# v=243 for ESC[1m (bold): near the bright end

# Looking at the jp2a code (from memory/documentation):
# The char for each pixel uses: palette_index = pixel_value * (palette_len - 1) / 255
# For grayscale ANSI output:
# - if pixel_value == 0 -> no-color (but still outputs ESC[37m for visibility on dark bg?)
# - if pixel_value high enough for 'W' or 'M' -> bold

# Wait! Let me check: does ESC[1m appear ONLY for 'W' and 'M' characters?
# Earlier I saw for jp2a.jpg --colors gave ESC[1m for W and M chars
# And for g1_243 (which maps to W = idx 21), we get ESC[1m
# For g1_250 (which maps to M = idx 22), we also get ESC[1m

# Let me check g1_238..249 more carefully:
for v in 235 236 237 238 239 240 241 242 243 244 245 246 247 248 249 250 251; do
    char=$(./executable --size=1x1 /tmp/g1_${v}.jpg 2>&1 | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n' | cut -c1-2)
    colors=$(./executable --size=1x1 --colors /tmp/g1_${v}.jpg 2>&1 | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
    echo "v=$v char=0x$char colors=$colors"
done

# Now let me understand the image resizing algorithm.
# The key question: how does jp2a map source pixels to output chars?
# We know the formula for char selection: round(lum * (n-1) / 255.0)
# But how is luminance computed?

# For 3-comp RGB: lum = 0.2989*R + 0.5866*G + 0.1145*B
# For 1-comp gray: lum = Y (the grayscale value)

# And for resizing: how does jp2a average pixels?
# The man page says: "jp2a skips some X-pixels along each scanline"
# And "jp2a does not interpolate when resizing"

# So the resize is done by SAMPLING, not averaging!
# jp2a probably samples a subset of source pixels for each output pixel

# Let me test this by looking at a simple case:
# For a 10x10 image output to 3x3:
# source pixel at (x_src, y_src) maps to output (x_out, y_out) where:
# x_src = x_out * src_width / out_width (approximately)
# y_src = y_out * src_height / out_height (approximately)

# Let me look at the luminance computation for color images:
# The default weights are: red=0.2989, green=0.5866, blue=0.1145
# Let me verify these by testing:

# Create a pure red image (255,0,0) and check what char we get

./executable --size=1x1 /tmp/test_green.jpg 2>&1 | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n'; echo ""

# JPEG decodes to exact values! (0,63,127,191,255)
# But jp2a gives: '.', ';', 'l', 'x', 'X'
# My formula gives: ' ', '.', 'l', 'O', 'M'
# 
# Position 4 (v=255): formula='M' (idx=22), actual='X' (idx=19)
# The actual 'X' corresponds to a LOWER luminance!
# 
# Hmm wait. Could the issue be that jp2a INVERTS (--invert) by default?
# Let me check: the default is --background=dark which means NO INVERT
# 
# With invert: palette[22-idx] instead of palette[idx]
# For v=255: inverted_idx = 22 - 22 = 0 -> ' '
# But actual is 'X' (idx=19)...
# 
# Let me look at this from a pure char perspective:
# The 5-pixel gradient (0,63,127,191,255) gives chars '.', ';', 'l', 'x', 'X'
# What lum values would give these chars?
python3 << 'EOF'
palette = "   ...',;:clodxkO0KXNWM"
n = len(palette)
chars = '.;lxX'
values = [0, 63, 127, 191, 255]
for i, (v, c) in enumerate(zip(values, chars)):
    idx = palette.index(c)
    ideal_lum = idx * 255.0 / (n-1)
    print(f"v={v}: char={c!r} idx={idx} ideal_lum={ideal_lum:.1f}")

# So for v=255, we get char 'X' (idx=19) which requires ideal_lum = 19*255/22 = 220.2
# BUT the actual pixel is 255!
# round(255*22/255) = 22 -> 'M' not 'X'!

# The difference: idx 22 vs 19. The actual is 3 lower.
# For v=191: char='x' (idx=14), ideal_lum = 14*255/22 = 162.3
#   But actual v=191! round(191*22/255) = round(16.5) = 17 -> '0', not 'x' (14)!

# The formula ROUND doesn't work! Let me try INT FLOOR:
print("\nTesting int(v*(n-1)/255) floor:")
for v, c in zip(values, chars):
    idx = int(v * (n-1) / 255)
    print(f"v={v}: formula={palette[idx]!r}(idx={idx}), actual={c!r}(idx={palette.index(c)})")

# And int(v*(n-1)/256) or similar
print("\nTesting int(v*(n-1)/256):")
for v, c in zip(values, chars):
    idx = int(v * (n-1) / 256)
    if idx >= n: idx = n-1
    print(f"v={v}: formula={palette[idx]!r}(idx={idx}), actual={c!r}(idx={palette.index(c)})")
EOF

#   Also: forward: 3*5%10=5 -> NOT
# out0 AND out1 ✓
# col3: out_x=1, backward: 3*5%10=5 -> NOT; forward: 4*5%10=0 -> YES! out_x=1 < 2 -> NO!
# ONLY out1 ✓
# col4: out_x=2, backward: 4*5%10=0 -> YES! out_x=2 <= 2 -> APPLY!
#   forward: 5*5%10=5 -> NOT
# out1 AND out2 ✓
# col5: out_x=2, backward: 5*5%10=5 -> NOT; forward: 6*5%10=0 -> YES! out_x=2 >= 2 -> APPLY!
# out2 AND out3 ✓
# col6: out_x=3, backward: 6*5%10=0 -> YES! But out_x=3 > 2 -> NO backward!
#   forward: 7*5%10=5 -> NOT
# ONLY out3 ✓
# col7: out_x=3, backward: 7*5%10=5 -> NOT; forward: 8*5%10=0 -> YES! out_x=3 >= 2 -> APPLY!
# out3 AND out4 ✓
# col8: out_x=4, backward: 8*5%10=0 -> YES! But out_x=4 > 2 -> NO backward!
#   forward: 9*5%10=5 -> NOT
# ONLY out4 ✓
# col9: out_x=4, backward: 9*5%10=5 -> NOT; forward: 10*5%10=0 -> YES! But out_x=4 = out_w-1 -> can't go to out_w! NO forward!
# ONLY out4 ✓
# 
# ALL MATCH! The algorithm is:
# For each source pixel at column src_x:
# out_x = src_x * out_w / src_w (floor)
# 1. ALWAYS accumulate into out_x (primary)
# 2. BACKWARD sharing: if src_x * out_w % src_w == 0 AND out_x > 0 AND out_x <= out_w/2:
#    Also accumulate into out_x - 1
# 3. FORWARD sharing: if (src_x+1) * out_w % src_w == 0 AND out_x < out_w-1 AND out_x >= out_w/2:
#    Also accumulate into out_x + 1
# 
# The midpoint out_w/2 might not be exactly integer for odd out_w...
# Let me verify the exact threshold with the 30->10 case!

# Verify for 30->10 (step=3):
src_w = 30
out_w = 10
threshold = out_w / 2  # = 5

for j in range(src_w):
    out_x = j * out_w // src_w
    bkwd = (j * out_w % src_w == 0) and (out_x > 0) and (out_x <= threshold)
    fwd = ((j+1) * out_w % src_w == 0) and (out_x < out_w-1) and (out_x >= threshold)
    
    assignments = [out_x]
    if bkwd: assignments.append(out_x - 1)
    if fwd: assignments.append(out_x + 1)
    
    if len(assignments) > 1:
        print(f"col {j}: out_x={out_x}, assignments={assignments}")
EOF

    echo "bright_row=$row: $result"
done

# Mine: ' ', ' ', '.', '.', '.', "'", ',', ';', ':', 'c', 'o', 'd', 'x', 'k', 'O', '0', 'K', 'X', 'N', 'W'
# Original: ' ', ' ', ' ', '.', '.', "'", ',', ';', ':', 'c', 'o', 'd', 'x', 'k', 'O', '0', 'X', 'N', 'W', 'M'
# 
# Differences: 
# Position 2: '.' vs ' ' - mine is shifted by 1!
# Position 16: 'K' vs 'X' - mine is shifted!
# Position 19: 'W' vs 'M' - mine is shifted!
# 
# Original has the SMALL GROUP at a DIFFERENT position than mine.
# 
# My algorithm: small group at out10 (starts at row 120)
# Original: seems to have small group at a different position (all chars shifted by 1)
# 
# Let me figure out what the ORIGINAL group sizes are:
# Original 1x20 output: ' ', ' ', ' ', '.', '.', "'", ',', ';', ':', 'c', 'o', 'd', 'x', 'k', 'O', '0', 'X', 'N', 'W', 'M'
# 
# For a gradient 0..255 over 240 rows, with step=12:
# Row at y for value v: v = y * 255 / 239
# For each output group, average value determines the char.
# 
# Let me compute expected average for each group and see what chars they give:
python3 << 'EOF'
palette = "   ...',;:clodxkO0KXNWM"
n = len(palette)
src_h = 240

# Original output chars:
orig = " " * 3 + "..',:clodxkO0XNWM"  # 20 chars (from output)
# Actually: ' ',' ',' ','.','.','\'',',',';',':','c','o','d','x','k','O','0','X','N','W','M'

# Let me manually extract from the original output
orig_chars = [' ', ' ', ' ', '.', '.', "'", ',', ';', ':', 'c', 'o', 'd', 'x', 'k', 'O', '0', 'X', 'N', 'W', 'M']
# 20 chars for 20 output rows

print("Expected avg for each char and implied group boundaries:")
for i, c in enumerate(orig_chars):
    idx = palette.index(c)
    ideal_avg = idx * 255.0 / (n-1)
    print(f"  out{i:2d}: char={c!r}(idx={idx}), ideal_avg={ideal_avg:.1f}")

# What rows would give these averages?
# row_val(y) = y * 255 / 239 ≈ y * 1.0669
print("\nFinding group start/end from averages:")
for i, c in enumerate(orig_chars):
    idx = palette.index(c)
    lo = (idx - 0.5) * 255.0 / (n-1)
    hi = (idx + 0.5) * 255.0 / (n-1)
    # avg_group = sum(row_vals) / count
    # We need: lo <= avg <= hi
    print(f"  out{i:2d}: char={c!r}, avg range [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f})")
EOF

# 
# So the original jp2a format is:
# - After palette line, the progress starts DIRECTLY (no blank line)
# - Each progress update uses \r (carriage return) to overwrite the line
# - The FIRST progress bar update starts with \r (so it goes after the palette line without newline!)

# Wait - but looking at this output, the first progress line starts with ^M (carriage return)

# Then the first "\rDecompressing image [...]" uses \r to position to start of a new line?
# No - \r goes to start of CURRENT line.
# 
# But since after \n we're on a new line, \r would go back to start of THAT new line.
# So "\nDecompressing image\r..." would:
# 1. Print palette line + newline (cursor now at start of next line)
# 2. Print Decompressing image [...
# 3. The \r in the NEXT update returns to start of SAME line

# - \r goes to start of line (the blank line after palette)
# - Then prints the progress
#

#

# Great! The compile.sh works correctly.
# 
# Let me also improve the compile.sh to be more robust for fresh checkouts:
cat > /workspace/compile.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
set -e

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"

# Find libjpeg library
LIBJPEG_PATH=""
for candidate in \
    "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjpeg.so.8" \
    "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjpeg.so.8.2.2" \
    "/usr/lib/libjpeg.so" \
    "/usr/local/lib/libjpeg.so"; do
    if [ -f "$candidate" ]; then
        LIBJPEG_PATH="$candidate"
        break
    fi
done

if [ -z "$LIBJPEG_PATH" ]; then
    echo "libjpeg not found, trying to install..."
    if command -v apt-get >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        apt-get install -y libjpeg-dev 2>/dev/null || \
        apt-get install -y libjpeg-turbo8-dev 2>/dev/null || \
        apt-get install -y libjpeg8-dev 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
    # Search again after install attempt
    LIBJPEG_PATH=$(find /usr -name "libjpeg.so*" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
fi

if [ -z "$LIBJPEG_PATH" ]; then
    echo "Error: libjpeg not found"
    exit 1
fi

LIBJPEG_DIR="$(dirname "$LIBJPEG_PATH")"

# Create a symlink if needed for linking
if [ ! -f "$LIBJPEG_DIR/libjpeg.so" ]; then
    # Try to use a temp symlink
    LINK_DIR="/tmp/jp2a_libs"
    mkdir -p "$LINK_DIR"
    ln -sf "$LIBJPEG_PATH" "$LINK_DIR/libjpeg.so"
    EXTRA_FLAGS="-L$LINK_DIR"
else
    EXTRA_FLAGS="-L$LIBJPEG_DIR"
fi

# Compile
gcc -O2 -o "$SCRIPT_DIR/executable" "$SCRIPT_DIR/src/jp2a.c" \
    $EXTRA_FLAGS \
    -ljpeg -lm \
    -Wl,-rpath,"$LIBJPEG_DIR" \
    2>&1

echo "Compilation successful: $SCRIPT_DIR/executable"
EOF
chmod +x /workspace/compile.sh
